Replay

Godot bridge performance assessment

5 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓
View ownershipCopy, codec and replay costsDecisions

Measurements on macOS arm64, Odin dev-2026-04, Godot 4.7.1, optimized native builds. These are isolated elapsed costs with fixed workloads, not rendered-frame rates, confidence intervals or a general guarantee for every game. Raw receipts, binaries' hashes, source hashes and workload details are in the delivery evidence.

View ownership#

The initial dense benchmark justified replacing repeated linear lookup and making root-property caching opt-in. The final comparison also includes small and sparse pools and the additional typed owner. Every timed frame moves x; rotation, scale, color and typed paint payload remain constant. Scenes are already instantiated. Typed paint is empty here, so real child painting can add game-specific work.

At 1,024 active views, the first expanded comparison measured original Nodes2 at 609.7 µs, indexing at 107.0 µs, cached Nodes2 at 45.05 µs and typed ownership at 70.58 µs per presentation call. Caching avoided roughly 75% of root property writes. Typed lifetime/payload bookkeeping adds work; ergonomics are not cost-free.

That comparison exposed a sparse regression: one active view in a capacity-1,024 pool still scanned capacity and cleared whole indexes. The final implementation tracks occupied buckets and uses a retained-membership path after full duplicate/ identity preflight. Sparse index clearing visits occupied buckets; dense clearing stays contiguous. Unchanged membership skips lifecycle/free-slot/index rebuilding. Reordered input is supported; changed membership uses the ordinary lifecycle path.

An alternating comparison of frozen before/after binaries measured:

Active / capacity Cached Nodes2 before → after, µs Typed owner before → after, µs
1 / 1 0.033 → 0.033 0.058 → 0.050
8 / 8 0.300 → 0.275 0.442 → 0.425
1 / 1,024 2.167 → 0.033 4.208 → 0.050
8 / 1,024 2.442 → 0.258 4.533 → 0.358
64 / 64 2.317 → 2.242 3.500 → 3.200
512 / 512 21.217 → 20.467 32.542 → 29.667
1,024 / 1,024 44.017 → 42.142 67.458 → 61.892

Each table cell is the median across three process medians, each with five timed 120-call batches after warmup. Very small values approach timer granularity; interpret broad changes rather than the last decimal. Indexed uncached dense 1,024-view calls also improved slightly, 106.08 → 103.08 µs. Counts match exactly. The two comparisons were separate runs; do not mix their numbers as one paired experiment. Membership churn/scene construction, GPU and rendering are excluded.

Memory increases: each index now retains four bytes per configured entry for its occupied-bucket list, in addition to its existing keys/values. Nodes2 owns two indexes; the typed owner owns two additional indexes and rig/value/batch storage. All remain presentation-only. Stable presentation calls allocate no Odin storage; scene entry/exit still creates and retires engine objects. Capacity scans remain when membership changes or owners clear/destroy.

Copy, codec and replay costs#

A second optimized benchmark uses actual Hello and Scrapyard models, a 32-byte selective display output, a 64-frame history and a 16-tick replay suffix. Scrapyard starts with two players and 40 mobs under the documented combat fixture. Medians:

Operation Hello Scrapyard
State bytes 960 61,536
Complete canonical bytes 896 52,608
Public canonical bytes 896 24,032
Materialized frame read 0.016 µs 0.926 µs
Ordinary read then selective projection 0.0013 µs 0.0012 µs
Detached replay.project 0.0131 µs 0.0108 µs
Authority encode / hash 0.331 / 0.141 µs 33.641 / 24.474 µs
Public encode / hash 0.335 / 0.131 µs 10.101 / 4.920 µs
Advance one tick 0.105 µs 11.351 µs
Replay 16 ticks 1.406 µs 149.332 µs

The selective projection timing intentionally permits optimizer elimination of unused fields. It is not evidence of physically copying 61 KB in a nanosecond. project has validation/reentry overhead; its primary benefit here is an explicit detached ownership contract, not a speedup over an optimized ordinary read. The materialized case retains every field and gives a useful separate copy cost. Hello's real full view-batch adapter expands its small World; it is an ergonomics example, not a smaller-buffer optimization.

Scrapyard's retained records and replay scratch each occupy 3,941,376 bytes at 64 frames, excluding separate events and allocator metadata. Default 128-frame retention roughly doubles those arrays. Immutable definition catalogs can remove truly static data from future Worlds, but the catalog/dependency lifetime must stay complete across replay, saves and migration. Cavecrawl intentionally still embeds its small baked definitions to preserve its existing checkpoint contract.

Decisions#

Implemented: indexed identity lookup, exclusive property caching/invalidation, changed-value paint, retained-membership fast paths and sparse index clearing. These reduce measured repeated work without changing gameplay assignments.

Keep detached projections for ownership/ergonomics; make no universal zero-copy promise. The measured copy cost does not justify introducing chunked/COW storage and mandatory mutation tracking now. Memory can still become significant for much larger Worlds/history; revisit with an actual target workload and a storage design that retains ordinary assignments and transactional replay.

Do not add a broad snapshot encoding/hash cache here. Inspection shows snapshot construction includes recipient projection, connection generation/serial, action settlement/input frontiers and per-recipient baselines. Private authority fields and public values are different contracts. Canonical bytes are already retained for delta baselines. Safe reuse requires explicit equality of all these dependencies; a frame tick alone is insufficient. Public encode/hash costs are material, but this bridge profile does not isolate a redundant network call to remove safely.

Existing opt-in exact correction reuse remains available under its documented full- dependency rules. This work leaves wire hashes, schemas, checkpoint versions and replay semantics unchanged. A future optimization must preserve those contracts or introduce an explicit compatibility change.
